# Wood & Long, LLC

> Wood & Long, LLC is a Columbus, Ohio law firm founded in 2014 by Jessica M. Wood and Chelsea L. Long. The firm practices only divorce and family law, including dissolution, custody, child and spousal support, civil protection orders, adoption, and post-decree matters, for clients across Central Ohio.

## Key facts
- Practice: divorce and family law only
- Founded: 2014, by Jessica M. Wood and Chelsea L. Long
- Office: 580 S. High St., Suite 230, Columbus, OH 43215
- Phone: (614) 567-3031
- Hours: Monday–Friday, 8:30 a.m.–5:00 p.m.
- Consultations: 90 minutes; In person at our Columbus office, Zoom, Phone; consultation fee credited toward fees if hired
- Areas served: Columbus and Central Ohio (Franklin County, Delaware County, Licking County, Fairfield County, Union County, Madison County, Pickaway County)
- Certification: Chelsea L. Long is a Certified Specialist in Family Relations Law, certified by the Ohio State Bar Association

## Practice areas
- [Child Custody](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/child-custody/): Ohio law calls custody the "allocation of parental rights and responsibilities." A court either names one parent the residential parent and legal custodian or approves a shared parenting plan, and every decision turns on the child's best interest under ORC 3109.04.
- [Child Support](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/child-support/): Ohio sets child support with a guideline worksheet under ORC Chapter 3119 that combines both parents' incomes and divides the cost of raising the child between them. Support usually lasts until 18, or until 19 if the child is still in high school, and can be changed when the recalculated amount differs by more than 10%.
- [Dissolution](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/dissolution/): A dissolution ends an Ohio marriage when both spouses agree on every issue before filing. You file a joint petition with a signed separation agreement covering property, debts, support and parenting, and the court holds a hearing 30 to 90 days later. If both spouses confirm under oath that they still agree, the court grants the dissolution.
- [Divorce](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/divorce/): A divorce ends an Ohio marriage through a court case filed by one spouse in the county Domestic Relations court. You must have lived in Ohio for at least six months, and you must show a legal ground, such as incompatibility or living apart for a year. The court then divides property and debts and decides support and parenting if the spouses cannot agree.
- [Grandparent Rights](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/grandparent-rights/): Ohio grandparents do not have an automatic right to see their grandchildren. They can ask a court for companionship or visitation only in certain situations set by ORC 3109.051, 3109.11 and 3109.12, and the court must give special weight to the parents' wishes. Seeking custody is harder and generally requires showing that the parents are unsuitable.
- [Guardian ad Litem](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/guardian-ad-litem/): A guardian ad litem (GAL) is a person the court appoints in a custody case to look into the facts and recommend what is in the child's best interest. In Ohio, a GAL does not represent either parent. The judge or magistrate makes the final decision, and parents can challenge a GAL's report through questioning at the hearing and objections.
- [LGBTQ+ Family Law](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/lgbtq-family-law/): Since Obergefell v. Hodges in 2015, same-sex couples in Ohio marry and divorce under the same laws as any other couple. Some issues need extra care, like dividing property for couples who were together before they could legally marry. Many LGBTQ+ parents also take steps such as adoption to make sure both parents' legal ties to their children are secure.
- [Mediation](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/mediation/): Family mediation is a private meeting where a neutral mediator helps you and the other party reach your own agreement on parenting, support or property. In Ohio, what is said in mediation is generally confidential under the Uniform Mediation Act. Mediation is voluntary in its outcome: nothing is final unless both sides agree and the court approves it.
- [Paternity](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/paternity/): When parents are not married, Ohio law does not recognize the father's legal relationship to a child until paternity is established under ORC Chapter 3111. That can happen through a signed acknowledgment, a CSEA genetic-testing order, or a juvenile court case. Paternity creates support duties, but custody and parenting time require separate court orders.
- [Post-Decree Modification](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/post-decree-modification/): After a divorce or custody case ends, Ohio courts can still change some orders when circumstances change. Custody changes require a change in circumstances and a finding that the change serves the child's best interest. Child support can be recalculated, and spousal support can be changed only if the court kept the power to do so.
- [Prenuptial Agreements](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/prenuptial-agreements/): A prenuptial agreement is a written contract two people sign before marriage that sets how property, debts and spousal support will be handled if the marriage ends. Since 2023, Ohio also allows married couples to sign postnuptial agreements. Either kind must be entered freely, with full financial disclosure, and without fraud, duress or overreaching to be enforced.
- [Property Division](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/property-division/): In an Ohio divorce or dissolution, the court first decides which property is marital and which is separate under ORC 3105.171. Separate property, such as what you owned before marriage or inherited, generally stays with you. Marital property and debts are divided equally unless an equal split would be unfair, in which case the court divides them in the way it finds equitable.
- [Protection Orders](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/protection-orders/): An Ohio domestic violence civil protection order is a court order that tells a family or household member to stay away and stop any abuse. You can ask for a temporary ex parte order on the same day you file, and the court then holds a full hearing where both sides can be heard. A final order can last up to five years.
- [Spousal Support](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/spousal-support/): Spousal support, often called alimony, is money one spouse pays the other during or after an Ohio divorce or legal separation. Ohio has no statewide formula. The court decides whether support is appropriate and reasonable, and how much and how long, by weighing the factors in ORC 3105.18, and it can change the award later only if the decree keeps that power.
- [Stepparent Adoption](https://www.woodlongfamilylaw.com/practice-areas/stepparent-adoption/): In Ohio, a stepparent adopts a spouse's child through the probate court under ORC Chapter 3107. The child's other legal parent usually must consent, unless that parent went at least a year without justifiable cause without more than minimal contact or required support. A final adoption ends the other parent's rights and duties and makes the stepparent a full legal parent.
